{{Short description|Partially ordered vector space, ordered as a lattice}}
{{redirect|Vector lattice||Lattice (disambiguation)}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''Riesz space''', '''lattice-ordered vector space''' or '''vector lattice''' is a [[Ordered vector space|partially ordered vector space]] where the [[order structure]] is a [[Lattice (order)|lattice]].

Riesz spaces are named after [[Frigyes Riesz]] who first defined them in his 1928 paper ''Sur la décomposition des opérations fonctionelles linéaires''.

Riesz spaces have wide-ranging applications. They are important in [[measure theory]], in that important results are special cases of results for Riesz spaces. For example, the [[Radon–Nikodym theorem]] follows as a special case of the [[Freudenthal spectral theorem]]. Riesz spaces have also seen application in [[mathematical economics]] through the work of Greek-American economist and mathematician [[Charalambos D. Aliprantis]].

== Definition ==

=== Preliminaries ===

If <math>X</math> is an [[ordered vector space]] (which by definition is a vector space over the [[Real number|reals]]) and if <math>S</math> is a subset of <math>X</math> then an element <math>b \in X</math> is an '''upper bound''' (resp. '''lower bound''') of <math>S</math> if <math>s \leq b</math> (resp. <math>s \geq b</math>) for all <math>s \in S.</math>
An element <math>a</math> in <math>X</math> is the '''least upper bound''' or '''[[supremum]]''' (resp. '''greater lower bound''' or '''[[infimum]]''') of <math>S</math> if it is an upper bound (resp. a lower bound) of <math>S</math> and if for any upper bound (resp. any lower bound) <math>b</math> of <math>S,</math>  <math>a \leq b</math> (resp. <math>a \geq b</math>).

=== Definitions ===

=== Preordered vector lattice ===

A '''preordered vector lattice''' is a [[preordered vector space]] <math>E</math> in which every pair of elements has a [[supremum]].

More explicitly, a '''preordered vector lattice''' is vector space endowed with a [[preorder]], <math>\,\leq,\,</math> such that for any <math>x, y, z \in E</math>:
# [[Translation invariance|Translation Invariance]]: <math>x \leq y</math> implies <math>x + z \leq y + z.</math>
# [[Homogeneous function#Positive homogeneity|Positive Homogeneity]]: For any scalar <math>0 \leq a,</math> <math>x \leq y</math> implies <math>a x \leq a y.</math>
# For any pair of vectors <math>x, y \in E,</math> there exists a [[supremum]] (denoted <math>x \vee y</math>) in <math>E</math> with respect to the order <math>\,(\leq).\,</math>

The preorder, together with items 1 and 2, which make it "compatible with the vector space structure", make <math>E</math> a preordered vector space. 
Item 3 says that the preorder is a [[join semilattice]]. 
Because the preorder is compatible with the vector space structure, one can show that any pair also have an [[infimum]], making <math>E</math> also a [[meet semilattice]], hence a lattice.

A preordered vector space <math>E</math> is a preordered vector lattice if and only if it satisfies any of the following equivalent properties: 
<ol>
<li>For any <math>x, y \in E,</math> their [[supremum]] exists in <math>E.</math></li>
<li>For any <math>x, y \in E,</math> their [[infimum]] exists in <math>E.</math></li>
<li>For any <math>x, y \in E,</math> their infimum and their supremum exist in <math>E.</math></li>
<li>For any <math>x \in E,</math> <math>\sup \{x, 0\}</math> exists in <math>E.</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein| 2011|pp=139-153}} </li>
</ol>

=== Riesz space and vector lattices ===

A '''Riesz space''' or a '''vector lattice''' is a preordered vector lattice whose preorder is a [[partial order]]. 
Equivalently, it is an [[ordered vector space]]
for which the ordering is a [[Lattice (order)|lattice]].

Note that many authors required that a vector lattice be a [[Partially ordered space|partially order]]ed vector space (rather than merely a preordered vector space) while others only require that it be a preordered vector space. 
We will henceforth assume that every Riesz space and every vector lattice is an [[ordered vector space]] but that a preordered vector lattice is not necessarily partially ordered.

If <math>E</math> is an ordered vector space over <math>\R</math> whose positive cone <math>C</math> (the elements <math>\,\geq 0</math>) is generating (that is, such that <math>E = C - C</math>), and if for every <math>x, y \in C</math> either <math>\sup\{x, y\}</math> or <math>\inf \{x, y\}</math> exists, then <math>E</math> is a vector lattice.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}}

=== Intervals ===

An '''order interval''' in a partially ordered vector space is a [[convex set]] of the form <math>[a, b] = \{ x : a \leq x \leq b \}.</math> 
In an ordered real vector space, every interval of the form <math>[-x, x]</math> is [[Balanced set|balanced]].{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}} 
From axioms 1 and 2 above it follows that <math>x, y \in [a, b]</math> and <math>t \in (0, 1)</math> implies <math>t x (1 - t) y \in [a, b].</math> 
A subset is said to be '''order bounded''' if it is contained in some order interval.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}} 
An '''[[order unit]]''' of a preordered vector space is any element <math>x</math> such that the set <math>[-x, x]</math> is [[Absorbing set|absorbing]].{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}}

The set of all [[linear functional]]s on a preordered vector space <math>V</math> that map every order interval into a bounded set is called the '''[[order bound dual]]''' of <math>V</math> and denoted by <math>V^b.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}} 
If a space is ordered then its order bound dual is a vector subspace of its [[algebraic dual]].

A subset <math>A</math> of a vector lattice <math>E</math> is called '''[[order complete]]''' if for every non-empty subset <math>B \subseteq A</math> such that <math>B</math> is order bounded in <math>A,</math> both <math>\sup B</math> and <math>\inf B</math> exist and are elements of <math>A.</math> 
We say that a vector lattice <math>E</math> is '''order complete''' if <math>E</math> is an order complete subset of <math>E.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204-214}}

== Classification ==
Finite-dimensional Riesz spaces are entirely classified by the [[Archimedean property]]:
:'''Theorem''':{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}} Suppose that <math>X</math> is a vector lattice of finite-dimension <math>n.</math> If <math>X</math> is [[Archimedean order]]ed then it is (a vector lattice) isomorphic to <math>\R^{n}</math> under its canonical order. Otherwise, there exists an integer <math>k</math> satisfying <math>2 \leq k \leq n</math> such that <math>X</math> is isomorphic to <math>\R^k_L \times \R^{n-k}</math> where <math>\R^{n-k}</math> has its canonical order, <math>\R^k_L</math> is <math>\R^k</math> with the [[lexicographical order]], and the product of these two spaces has the canonical product order.

The same result does not hold in infinite dimensions.  For an example due to [[Irving Kaplansky|Kaplansky]], consider the vector space {{mvar|V}} of functions on {{closed-closed|0,1}} that are continuous except at finitely many points, where they have a [[Zeros and poles|pole]] of second order.  This space is lattice-ordered by the usual pointwise comparison, but cannot be written as {{math|{{mathbb|R}}<sup>&kappa;</sup>}} for any [[cardinal number|cardinal]] {{math|&kappa;}}.{{sfn|Birkhoff|1967|p=240}}  On the other hand, [[Regular category#Epi-mono factorization|epi-mono factorization]] in the category of {{math|{{mathbb|R}}}}-vector spaces also applies to Riesz spaces: every lattice-ordered vector space [[injective function|injects]] into a quotient of {{math|{{mathbb|R}}<sup>&kappa;</sup>}} by a [[solid set|solid]] subspace.<ref>Fremlin, ''Measure Theory'', claim 352L.</ref>

== Basic properties ==

Every Riesz space is a [[Ordered vector space|partially ordered vector space]], but not every partially ordered vector space is a Riesz space.

Note that for any subset <math>A</math> of <math>X,</math> <math>\sup A = - \inf (-A)</math> whenever either the supremum or infimum exists (in which case they both exist).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}}
If <math>x \geq 0</math> and <math>y \geq 0</math> then <math>[0, x] + [0, y] = [0, x + y].</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}} 
For all <math>a, b, x, \text{ and } y</math> in a Riesz space <math>X,</math> <math>a - \inf (x, y) + b = \sup (a - x + b, a - y + b).</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204-214}}

=== Absolute value ===

For every element <math>x</math> in a Riesz space <math>X,</math> the '''absolute value''' of <math>x,</math> denoted by <math>|x|,</math> is defined to be <math>| x|:= \sup \{x, -x\},</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204-214}} where this satisfies <math>-|x| \leq x \leq |x|</math> and <math>|x| \geq 0.</math> 
For any <math>x, y \in X</math> and any real number <math>r,</math> we have <math>|r x| = |r| |x|</math> and <math>|x + y| \leq |x| + |y|.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204-214}}

=== Disjointness ===

{{Main|Lattice disjoint}}

Two elements <math>x \text{ and } y</math> in a vector lattice <math>X</math> are said to be '''lattice disjoint''' or '''disjoint''' if <math>\inf \{|x|, |y|\} = 0,</math> in which case we write <math>x \perp y.</math> 
Two elements <math>x \text{ and } y</math> are disjoint if and only if <math>\sup\{|x|, |y|\} = |x| + |y|.</math> 
If <math>x \text{ and } y</math> are disjoint then <math>| x + y|=|x|+|y |</math> and <math>(x + y)^+ = x^+ + y^+,</math> where for any element <math>z,</math> <math>z^+ := \sup \{z, 0\}</math> and <math>z^- := \sup \{-z, 0\}.</math> 
We say that two sets <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are '''disjoint''' if <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are disjoint for all <math>a \in A</math> and all <math>b \in B,</math> in which case we write <math>A \perp B.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}} 
If <math>A</math> is the singleton set <math>\{ a \}</math> then we will write <math>a \perp B</math> in place of <math>\{a\} \perp B.</math> 
For any set <math>A,</math> we define the '''disjoint complement''' to be the set <math>A^{\perp} := \left\{ x \in X : x \perp A \right\}.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}} 
Disjoint complements are always [[Band (order theory)|bands]], but the converse is not true in general. 
If <math>A</math> is a subset of <math>X</math> such that <math>x = \sup A</math> exists, and if <math>B</math> is a subset lattice in <math>X</math> that is disjoint from <math>A,</math> then <math>B</math> is a lattice disjoint from <math>\{x\}.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}}

=== Representation as a disjoint sum of positive elements ===

For any <math>x \in X,</math> let <math>x^+ := \sup \{x, 0\}</math> and <math>x^- := \sup \{-x, 0\},</math> where note that both of these elements are <math>\geq 0</math> and <math>x = x^+ - x^-</math> with <math>|x|= x^+ + x^-.</math>  
Then <math>x^+</math> and <math>x^{-}</math> are disjoint, and <math>x = x^+ - x^-</math> is the unique representation of <math>x</math> as the difference of disjoint elements that are <math>\geq 0.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}} 
For all <math>x, y \in X,</math> <math>\left|x^+ - y^+\right| \leq|x - y|</math> and <math>x + y = \sup \{x, y\} + \inf \{x, y\}.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}} 
If <math>y \geq 0</math> and <math>x \leq y</math> then <math>x^+ \leq y.</math> 
Moreover, <math>x \leq y</math> if and only if <math>x^+ \leq y^+</math> and <math>x^- \leq y^-.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=74-78}}

Every Riesz space is a [[distributive lattice]]; that is, it has the following equivalent<ref group=Note>The conditions are equivalent only when they apply to all triples in a lattice.  There are elements in (for example) {{math|''N''<sub>5</sub>}} that satisfy the first equation but not the second.</ref> properties:<ref>{{cite book| last=Birkhoff|first=Garrett|author-link=Garrett Birkhoff|title=Lattice Theory|year=1967|edition=3rd|publisher=American Mathematical Society|series=Colloquium Publications|isbn=0-8218-1025-1|page=11}} §6, Theorem 9</ref> for all <math>x, y, z \in X</math>
# <math>x \wedge (y \vee z) = (x \wedge y) \vee (x \wedge z)</math> 
# <math>x \vee (y \wedge z) = (x \vee y) \wedge (x \vee z)</math>
# <math>(x \wedge y) \vee (y \wedge z) \vee (z \wedge x) = (x \vee y) \wedge (y \vee z) \wedge (z \vee x).</math>
# <math>x \wedge z = y \wedge z</math> and <math>x \vee z = y \vee z</math> always imply <math>x = y.</math>

Every Riesz space has the [[Approximately finite-dimensional C*-algebra#The Effros-Handelman-Shen theorem|Riesz decomposition property]].

== Order convergence ==

There are a number of meaningful non-equivalent ways to define convergence of sequences or nets with respect to the order structure of a Riesz space. A sequence <math>\left\{x_n\right\}</math> in a Riesz space <math>E</math> is said to '''converge monotonely''' if it is a [[Monotone sequence|monotone]] decreasing (resp. increasing) sequence and its [[infimum]] (supremum) <math>x</math> exists in <math>E</math> and denoted <math>x_n \downarrow x</math> (resp. <math>x_n \uparrow x</math>).

A sequence <math>\left\{x_n\right\}</math> in a Riesz space <math>E</math> is said to '''converge in order''' to <math>x</math> if there exists a monotone converging sequence <math>\left\{p_n\right\}</math> in <math>E</math> such that <math>\left|x_n - x\right| < p_n \downarrow 0.</math>

If <math>u</math> is a positive element of a Riesz space <math>E</math> then a sequence <math>\left\{ x_n \right\}</math> in <math>E</math> is said to '''converge u-uniformly''' to <math>x</math> if for any <math>r > 0</math> there exists an <math>N</math> such that <math>\left|x_n - x\right| < r u</math> for all <math>n > N.</math>

== Subspaces ==

The extra structure provided by these spaces provide for distinct kinds of Riesz subspaces. 
The collection of each kind structure in a Riesz space (for example, the collection of all ideals) forms a [[distributive lattice]].

=== Sublattices ===

If <math>X</math> is a vector lattice then a '''vector sublattice''' is a vector subspace <math>F</math> of <math>X</math> such that for all <math>x, y \in F,</math> <math>\sup\{x, y\}</math> belongs to <math>F</math> (where this supremum is taken in <math>X</math>).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204-214}} 
It can happen that a subspace <math>F</math> of <math>X</math> is a vector lattice under its canonical order but is {{em|not}} a vector sublattice of <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204-214}}

=== Ideals ===

{{Main|Solid set}}

A vector subspace <math>I</math> of a Riesz space <math>E</math> is called an '''ideal''' if it is '''[[Solid set|solid]]''', meaning if for <math>f \in I</math> and <math>g \in E,</math> <math>|g| \leq |f|</math> implies that <math>g \in I.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204-214}} 
The intersection of an arbitrary collection of ideals is again an ideal, which allows for the definition of a smallest ideal containing some non-empty subset <math>A</math> of <math>E,</math> and is called the ideal '''generated''' by <math>A.</math> An Ideal generated by a singleton is called a '''principal ideal'''.

=== Bands and σ-Ideals ===

{{Main|Band (order theory)}}

A '''band''' <math>B</math> in a Riesz space <math>E</math> is defined to be an ideal with the extra property, that for any element <math>f \in E</math> for which its absolute value <math>|f|</math> is the supremum of an arbitrary subset of positive elements in <math>B,</math> that <math>f</math> is actually in <math>B.</math> <math>\sigma</math>-''Ideals'' are defined similarly, with the words 'arbitrary subset' replaced with 'countable subset'. Clearly every band is a <math>\sigma</math>-ideal, but the converse is not true in general.

The intersection of an arbitrary family of bands is again a band. 
As with ideals, for every non-empty subset <math>A</math> of <math>E,</math> there exists a smallest band containing that subset, called {{em|the band generated by <math>A.</math>}} 
A band generated by a singleton is called a '''principal band'''.

=== Projection bands ===

A band <math>B</math> in a Riesz space, is called a '''projection band''', if <math>E = B \oplus B^{\bot},</math> meaning every element <math>f \in E</math> can be written uniquely as a sum of two elements, <math>f = u + v</math> with <math>u \in B</math> and <math>v \in B^{\bot}.</math> 
There then also exists a positive linear idempotent, or {{em|projection}}, <math>P_B : E \to E,</math> such that <math>P_B(f) = u.</math>

The collection of all projection bands in a Riesz space forms a [[Boolean algebra]]. Some spaces do not have non-trivial projection bands (for example, <math>C([0, 1])</math>), so this Boolean algebra may be trivial.

=== Completeness ===

A vector lattice is '''complete''' if every subset has both a supremum and an infimum.

A vector lattice is '''[[Dedekind complete]]''' if each set with an upper bound has a supremum and each set with a lower bound has an infimum.

An order complete, regularly ordered vector lattice whose canonical image in its [[order bidual]] is order complete is called '''minimal''' and is said to be '''of minimal type'''.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204–214}}

== Subspaces, quotients, and products ==

'''Sublattices'''

If <math>M</math> is a vector subspace of a preordered vector space <math>X</math> then the canonical ordering on <math>M</math> induced by <math>X</math>'s positive cone <math>C</math> is the preorder induced by the pointed convex cone <math>C \cap M,</math> where this cone is proper if <math>C</math> is proper (that is, if <math>C \cap (- C) = \varnothing</math>).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}}

A '''sublattice''' of a vector lattice <math>X</math> is a vector subspace <math>M</math> of <math>X</math> such that for all <math>x, y \in M,</math> <math>\sup_{}{}_X (x, y)</math> belongs to <math>X</math> (importantly, note that this supremum is taken in <math>X</math> and not in <math>M</math>).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}} 
If <math>X = L^p([0, 1], \mu)</math> with <math>0 < p < 1,</math> then the 2-dimensional vector subspace <math>M</math> of <math>X</math> defined by all maps of the form <math>t \mapsto a t + b</math> (where <math>a, b \in \R</math>) is a vector lattice under the induced order but is {{em|not}} a sublattice of <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}} 
This despite <math>X</math> being an [[order complete]] [[Archimedean order]]ed [[topological vector lattice]]. 
Furthermore, there exist vector a vector sublattice <math>N</math> of this space <math>X</math> such that <math>N \cap C</math> has empty interior in <math>X</math> but no positive linear functional on <math>N</math> can be extended to a positive linear functional on <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}}

'''Quotient lattices'''

Let <math>M</math> be a vector subspace of an ordered vector space <math>X</math> having positive cone <math>C,</math> let <math>\pi : X \to X / M</math> be the canonical projection, and let <math>\hat{C} := \pi(C).</math> 
Then <math>\hat{C}</math> is a cone in <math>X / M</math> that induces a canonical preordering on the [[Quotient space (linear algebra)|quotient space]] <math>X / M.</math> 
If <math>\hat{C}</math> is a proper cone in <math>X / M</math> then <math>\hat{C}</math> makes <math>X / M</math> into an ordered vector space.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}} 
If <math>M</math> is [[Cone-saturated|<math>C</math>-saturated]] then <math>\hat{C}</math> defines the canonical order of <math>X / M.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}} 
Note that <math>X=\R^2_{0}</math> provides an example of an ordered vector space where <math>\pi(C)</math> is not a proper cone.

If <math>X</math> is a vector lattice and <math>N</math> is a [[Solid set|solid]] vector subspace of <math>X</math> then <math>\hat{C}</math> defines the canonical order of <math>X / M</math> under which <math>L / M</math> is a vector lattice and the canonical map <math>\pi : X \to X / M</math> is a vector lattice homomorphism. 
Furthermore, if <math>X</math> is [[order complete]] and <math>M</math> is a band in <math>X</math> then <math>X / M</math> is isomorphic with <math>M^{\bot}.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}} 
Also, if <math>M</math> is solid then the [[Order topology (functional analysis)|order topology]] of <math>X / M</math> is the quotient of the order topology on <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}}

If <math>X</math> is a [[topological vector lattice]] and <math>M</math> is a closed [[Solid set|solid]] sublattice of <math>X</math> then <math>X / L</math> is also a topological vector lattice.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}}

'''Product'''

If <math>S</math> is any set then the space <math>X^S</math> of all functions from <math>S</math> into <math>X</math> is canonically ordered by the proper cone <math>\left\{ f \in X^S : f(s) \in C \text{ for all } s \in S \right\}.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}}

Suppose that <math>\left\{ X_\alpha : \alpha \in A \right\}</math> is a family of preordered vector spaces and that the positive cone of <math>X_\alpha</math> is <math>C_\alpha.</math> 
Then <math>C := \prod_{\alpha} C_\alpha</math> is a pointed convex cone in <math>\prod_\alpha X_\alpha,</math> which determines a canonical ordering on <math>\prod_\alpha X_\alpha</math>; 
<math>C</math> is a proper cone if all <math>C_\alpha</math> are proper cones.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}}

'''Algebraic direct sum'''

The algebraic [[direct sum]] <math>\bigoplus_\alpha X_\alpha</math> of <math>\left\{ X_\alpha : \alpha \in A \right\}</math> is a vector subspace of <math>\prod_\alpha X_\alpha</math> that is given the canonical subspace ordering inherited from <math>\prod_\alpha X_\alpha.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}}
If <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n</math> are ordered vector subspaces of an ordered vector space <math>X</math> then <math>X</math> is the ordered direct sum of these subspaces if the canonical algebraic isomorphism of <math>X</math> onto <math>\prod_\alpha X_{\alpha}</math> (with the canonical product order) is an [[order isomorphism]].{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}}

== Spaces of linear maps ==

A cone <math>C</math> in a vector space <math>X</math> is said to be '''generating''' if <math>C - C</math> is equal to the whole vector space.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}} 
If <math>X</math> and <math>W</math> are two non-trivial ordered vector spaces with respective positive cones <math>P</math> and <math>Q,</math> then <math>P</math> is generating in <math>X</math> if and only if the set <math>C = \{ u \in \operatorname{L}(X; W) : u(P) \subseteq Q \}</math> is a proper cone in <math>\operatorname{L}(X; W),</math> which is the space of all linear maps from <math>X</math> into <math>W.</math> 
In this case the ordering defined by <math>C</math> is called the '''canonical ordering''' of <math>\operatorname{L}(X; W).</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}} 
More generally, if <math>M</math> is any vector subspace of <math>\operatorname{L}(X; W)</math> such that <math>C \cap M</math> is a proper cone, the ordering defined by <math>C \cap M</math> is called the '''canonical ordering''' of <math>M.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}}

A linear map <math>u : X \to Y</math> between two preordered vector spaces <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> with respective positive cones <math>C</math> and <math>D</math> is called '''positive''' if <math>u(C) \subseteq D.</math> 
If <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are vector lattices with <math>Y</math> [[order complete]] and if <math>H</math> is the set of all positive linear maps from <math>X</math> into <math>Y</math> then the subspace <math>M := H - H</math> of <math>\operatorname{L}(X; Y)</math> is an order complete vector lattice under its canonical order; 
furthermore, <math>M</math> contains exactly those linear maps that map order intervals of <math>X</math> into order intervals of <math>Y.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}}

=== Positive functionals and the order dual ===

A linear function <math>f</math> on a preordered vector space is called '''positive''' if <math>x \geq 0</math> implies <math>f(x) \geq 0.</math> 
The set of all positive linear forms on a vector space, denoted by <math>C^*,</math> is a cone equal to the [[Polar set|polar]] of <math>- C.</math> 
The '''[[Order dual (functional analysis)|order dual]]''' of an ordered vector space <math>X</math> is the set, denoted by <math>X^+,</math> defined by <math>X^+ := C^* - C^*.</math> 
Although <math>X^+ \subseteq X^b,</math> there do exist ordered vector spaces for which set equality does {{em|not}} hold.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–209}}

== Vector lattice homomorphism ==

Suppose that <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are preordered vector lattices with positive cones <math>C</math> and <math>D</math> and let <math>u : X \to Y</math> be a map.  
Then <math>u</math> is a '''preordered vector lattice homomorphism''' if <math>u</math> is linear and if any one of the following equivalent conditions hold:{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–214}}{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}} 
<ol>
<li><math>u</math> preserves the lattice operations</li>
<li><math>u(\sup \{x, y\}) = \sup \{ u(x), u(y) \}</math> for all <math>x, y \in X.</math></li>
<li><math>u(\inf \{x, y\}) = \inf \{ u(x), u(y) \}</math> for all <math>x, y \in X.</math></li>
<li><math>u(|x|) = \sup \left\{ u\left(x^+\right), u\left(x^-\right) \right\}</math> for all <math>x \in X.</math></li>
<li><math>0 = \inf \left\{ u\left(x^+\right), u\left(x^-\right) \right\}</math> for all <math>x \in X.</math></li>
<li><math>u(C) = D</math> and <math>u^{-1}(0)</math> is a [[Solid set|solid]] subset of <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}}</li>
</ol>

A pre-ordered vector lattice homomorphism that is bijective is a '''pre-ordered vector lattice isomorphism'''.

A pre-ordered vector lattice homomorphism between two Riesz spaces is called a '''vector lattice homomorphism'''; 
if it is also bijective, then it is called a '''vector lattice isomorphism'''.

If <math>u</math> is a non-zero linear functional on a vector lattice <math>X</math> with positive cone <math>C</math> then the following are equivalent:
<ol>
<li><math>u : X \to \R</math> is a surjective vector lattice homomorphism.</li>
<li><math>0 = \inf \left\{ u\left(x^+\right), u\left(x^-\right) \right\}</math> for all <math>x \in X.</math></li>
<li><math>u \geq 0</math> and <math>u^{-1}(0)</math> is a [[Solid set|solid]] hyperplane in <math>X.</math></li>
<li><math>u'</math> generates an extreme ray of the cone <math>X^*</math> in <math>X^*.</math>
</ol>
An '''extreme ray''' of the cone <math>C</math> is a set <math>\{ r x : r \geq 0 \}</math> where <math>x \in C,</math> <math>x</math> is non-zero, and if <math>y \in C</math> is such that <math>x - y \in C</math> then <math>y = s x</math> for some <math>s</math> such that <math>0 \leq s \leq 1.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=205–214}}

A vector lattice homomorphism from <math>X</math> into <math>Y</math> is a [[topological homomorphism]] when <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are given their respective [[Order topology (functional analysis)|order topologies]].{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}}

== Projection properties ==

There are numerous projection properties that Riesz spaces may have. A Riesz space is said to have the (principal) projection property if every (principal) band is a projection band.

The so-called '''main inclusion theorem''' relates the following additional properties to the (principal) projection property:<ref>{{cite book|last1=Luxemburg|first1=W.A.J.|last2=Zaanen|first2=A.C.|title=Riesz Spaces : Vol. 1.|date=1971|publisher=North Holland|location=London|isbn=0720424518|pages=122–138|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QR4WhI7u7N4C|access-date=8 January 2018}}</ref> A Riesz space is...
* [[Dedekind-complete|Dedekind Complete (DC)]] if every nonempty set, bounded above, has a [[supremum]];
* Super Dedekind Complete (SDC) if every nonempty set, bounded above, has a countable subset with identical supremum;
* Dedekind <math>\sigma</math>-complete if every countable nonempty set, bounded above, has a supremum; and
* [[Archimedean ordered vector space|Archimedean property]] if, for every pair of positive elements <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, whenever the inequality <math>n x \leq y</math> holds for all integers <math>n</math>, <math>x = 0</math>.
Then these properties are related as follows.  SDC implies DC; DC implies both Dedekind <math>\sigma</math>-completeness and the projection property; Both Dedekind <math>\sigma</math>-completeness and the projection property separately imply the principal projection property; and the principal projection property implies the [[Archimedean property]].

None of the reverse implications hold, but Dedekind <math>\sigma</math>-completeness and the projection property together imply DC.

== Examples ==

* The space of continuous real valued functions with [[compact support]] on a topological space <math>X</math> with the [[pointwise]] [[partial order]] defined by <math>f \leq g</math> when <math>f(x) \leq g(x)</math> for all <math>x \in X,</math> is a Riesz space. It is Archimedean, but usually does not have the principal projection property unless <math>X</math> satisfies further conditions (for example, being [[extremally disconnected]]).
* Any [[Lp space|<math>L^p</math> space]] with the ([[almost everywhere]]) pointwise partial order is a Dedekind complete Riesz space.
* The space <math>\R^2</math> with the [[lexicographical order]] is a non-Archimedean Riesz space.

== Properties ==

* Riesz spaces are [[lattice ordered group]]s
* Every Riesz space is a [[distributive lattice]]
